To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1), 36 % of Uruguay’s continental territory has been converted to agricultural land (28% cropland, 8% exotic forests) in the last two decades, (2), 51 cells of 302 cells (17%) are priority areas for the conservation of vertebrates, and (3), 45% of priority cells will probably be lost by 2030, especially in four grassland ecoregions with high agricultural expansion.
the loss of natural grassland in Uruguay, driven by the expansion of agricultural lands, is the greatest threat of biodiversity loss in the country.

the conversion of grasslands to croppands and exotic forest plantation is the major threat to biodiversity in Uruguayan native grasslands, and that the top 17% most vulnerable sites for vertebrate and plant species should be prioritized for conservation.

the expansion of croplands and exotic forest plant species is the main threat to biodiversity in Uruguay, and that the most vulnerable sites are located in the north and east of the country.

the conservation of biodiversity in Uruguay is a matter of concern, since the expansion of cropland and exotic forest plantation is expected to increase the loss of grasslands in the next decades, with negative impacts on the diversity of vertebrate and plant species.
the expansion of agriculture and forestry plantations in the Uruguayan grassland ecoregions is a serious threat to the conservation of biodiversity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the conservation and management of natural grassland ecosystems in Uruguay, as in other countries with similar land-use dynamics, is urgent and necessary to preserve biodiversity and ecosystem services.
the loss of grasslands is a serious problem that threatens the conservation of biodiversity in Uruguay.
